comments.author: swatcoder
comments.text:
Is it forcing us to "pay off" technical debt or is it starting us on a compulsory endless treadmill of feature-neutral fix-work? Collectively, we just won't know for a while.
It totally feels like the former if you watch it find and fix vulnerabilities or other debt-tasks one after another.
But only so many of these "technical debt" issue are little off-by-one errors that get remedied by a surgically narrow patch.
Many enough require some kind of restructuring or redevelopment of their own and it's going to take time to figure out if AI faces the same dilemma as human developers: where each non-trivial change carries the risk of some new issue, ad infinitum.
If that happens to be the case, and AI isn't able to magically produce perfect software in finite time, then what's really happened is that the threat of hostile AI
exploiting
our technical debt will force us to always be burning and churning code just to remain a moving target.
It's another "we'll see" thing for now, I think.

stories.title_en: A new Go API for JSON

comments.author: modulovalue
comments.text:
I'm working on better SIMD support in Dart and one of the motivations for that work is specializing parser specifications based on schema specifications of that language.
Or more concretely, if we had a parser generator + json parser specification that can generate efficient simdjson style parsers, then we should be able to parse json restricted to a subset of json based on a schema at least as efficiently as simdjson can parse general purpose json.
That way we could have the best of both worlds, a (potentially lazy) statically type-safe model and simdjson performance!
I still think that this is definitely doable, it's just that a lot of infrastructure needs to be built for it.
I remember reading that Meta is doing something similar with binary formats. I find it weird that there's nothing like that for json yet.

comments.author: neuwirth
comments.text:

comments.author: nemo1618
comments.text:
For open-weight models, provable inference is trivial: just redo the computation! This is much faster, cheaper, and doesn't require any fancy cryptography, just deterministic inference (which, if you read carefully, the ZKP approach needs too). See
https://lukechampine.com/repligraphs
Of course, it's unlikely that we'll get open-weight models from OpenAI or Anthropic any time soon. That means we have to choose between a) fancy ZKPs, b) signed responses, or c) comparing results from multiple inference providers.
Whatever method ends up being used, it's clear to me that
some
form of provable inference is inevitable. People haven't caught on to its more significant applications, but they will. (This post touches upon one of them: model-driven audits.) Think about it:
we can prove that a particular mind authored a particular artifact.
That's never been possible before! You can't prove that Melville wrote Moby Dick, for example; but you
can
prove that Claude wrote a poem, or that Gemini approved a pull request, or that GPT got a particular score on some eval. This is a more powerful primitive than a cryptographic signature.

comments.text:
> In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers?
> the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.
> The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's check
I know they mentioned $ETH in the technical report, but this is exactly the mechanic for a crypto currency Proof-of-Work which is expensive by design.
When they announced it, I was hoping for a 5% overhead validation that the model that served you is really Fable and not Opus.
The quantization bit caught me out, because we saw the boundary crossing from good-context-size to bad is so sharp it feels like longer context requests are sent to quantized models to make more room for more KV-Cache. This would expose those sorts of tricks people can play to have the same GPU do better on short context benchmarks and gracefully degrade on long context.
At work, we did a bit of digging[1] into exactly why BaseTen, Fireworks and Together serve Inkling weights

comments.author: vessenes
comments.text:
I've been writing about the need for provable inference (and training) on and off for a number of years; this is welcome news and a good start, and a significant improvement on prior zk results.
The problems of inference proof for a closed model provider are more difficult than an open model provider -- you can get a probabilistic proof much more cheaply out of four independent inference providers running the same non-batched prompt than this 90-100x compute hit.
Anthropic and others also have a significant problem with these proofs in that they have a lot of incentive internally to have some portions of the pre-prompt secret; I haven't read this newest scheme closely enough to determine if they have a way to hide parts of the prompt with the proof. But if they don't, they are almost certainly not going to want to send these proofs out in the general case.
Last, I'll take this moment to soapbox and say for the researchers out there -- provable inference is nice. Provable training corpus information would be spectacular. It would be very, very, very nice to provide a set of model weights and a proof that they had only been trained on a dataset. To be clear, this is a really hard pro

comments.author: vintagedave
comments.text:
I've read that providers like those you find on OpenRouter can sometimes route to other models; this would catch that.
But I've also heard, as complete rumour, sometimes some named models perform significantly worse on some hosts and the theory is they're running quantized, without that being published. Would this solve that? The post mentions proving a set of weights, but not how those are represented? What would stop a host using true weights for generating the signature, while running on quantized versions?
>
We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position...
So, no...?

comments.author: ajb
comments.text: Interesting, but I'm not sure the property it attests is one we care about that much. Or rather, it's one you'd expect Anthropic not to tell you it needs to prove.  I mean it tells you that you're not being stiffed by Anthropic using a cheaper model and that they haven't literally been MiTMd, but that's kind of table stakes. Otherwise it's not telling you much useful. It's not telling you that your data hasn't been exfiltrated, and it's not telling you any useful property of the answer.

comments.author: xpct
comments.text:
> As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves ... how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers?
I find this a bit odd and backwards. Why do we choose not to make the deployment code to be robust, but instead to observe the model inference as proven? This moves unobservability layer to the system that collects the proofs. Given the assumption that code is fluid and LLMs are rewriting it often, how can we know it isn't being abused against the observer?
Goes without saying, it's also disappointing that this has nothing to do with making the model inference observable for consumers.

comments.author: grey-area
comments.text:
At first I thought this was work on the far more important problem of proving that LLM output is provable and correct given some source of truth. But it's about the trivial problem of 'proving' which model is being used.
Who will find this useful? I can't really think of a use for it, because if you don't trust the provider of your models, it's game over really - you're already giving them all sorts of private data, you're relying on their service, you have to trust them to some extent and this doesn't really help because unless you are running the service yourself. comments.author: heisenzombie
comments.text:
Regarding adding higher level functions to spreadsheets in general. For people using Excel (at least, a modern-ish version that has LAMBDA), LLMs are shockingly good at writing LAMBDA functions. Especially if you have the “Advanced Formula Environment”, which lets you write whole modules of multi-line functions in text files.
I’m personally allergic to ever using macros in Excel, and this is basically a better version of that for many (not all) purposes.
For a stupid example, I had Opus write a bunch of linear algebra functions, including stuff like computing eigenvectors, culminating in a single function that computes rotation matrices for point-cloud best-fitting (ie the procrustes problem). Yes, I’m fully aware it’s sort of cursed to do that, yes it works, and yes normal people can use the resulting spreadsheet fine, they just magically have an ALIGN3D(frompoints, topoints) function.
